full_judgment:
This appeal by the plaintiffs is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the „ Additional District Judge; Pabna in O.C. Appeal No. 63 of 1977 reversing the judgment and decree passed by the Munsif, 3rd Court in O.C. Suit No. 114 of 1969 and dismissing the suit. The plaintiffs brought the suit for a permanent injunction to restrain the defendants from disturbing the plaintiffs' possession of the suit land. The suit was in respect of 4 schedules of lands namely schedules Ka to Gha. 

 2. The plaintiffs' case was that the lands of schedule Ka belonged to Mojibor Rahman and Rajah Ali from whom the plaintiffs purchased the said lands by two kabalas dated 26.6.67 and 19.6.67. Lands of schedule Kha belonged to Hakimuddin and 7 others from whom the plaintiffs purchased the said land by 7 kabalas. The lands of schedule Ga belonged to Kalipada and Shyamapada who exchanged the said lands with Ataur Rahman by executing power of Attorney dated 6.8.65 and from Ataur Rahman the plaintiffs purchased the said lands by two kabalas dated 21.4.66 and 23.4.66. After their said purchase one Belal Hossein claimed right by an earlier settlement from Shyamapada and Katipada and to avoid the dispute the plaintiffs again purchased the same lands from Belal Hossain by two kabalas dated 1.1.68. Lands of Schedule Cha belonged to Landlord Prangobinda Chowdhury and others. As the said land accreted after the river receded towards the east Dr. Mojibor Rahman and others got tight by settlement from the said landlords by amalnamas and from them the plaintiffs purchased the said lands by 9 kabalas. Since their purchases the plaintiffs have been in possession of the said land on regular payment of rents by setting up a milk producing Co-operative Society and by growing Khasari, Kalai and other fodders. The defendants having no title or possession in the suit lands wrongfully threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs by destroying their khasari crops on 27.11.69 giving the cause for the suit. 

 3. The defendant No. 18 by one written statement and defendants 12 to 17 by a joint written statement contested the suit separately. The defendant No. 18 claimed right and possession only in schedule Ga land upon the plea that he along with Amanullah and others got the land by exchange with Kalipada and Shyamapada who executed power of attorney in their favour on 26.9.66. Defendants 12 to 17 claimed right and possession only in the schedule Gha lands upon the assertion that the said lands were their paternal lends and they exercised right and possession therein after the recession of the river. Thus these defendants in two sets denied the title and possession of the plaintiffs and asserted their title and possession only in schedule Ca and Gha lands. They also pleaded that the suit is unmaintainable. 4. The plaintiffs produced all the purchase deeds referred by them as well as amalnama, rent receipts. S.A. record and other documents while the defendant No. 18 produced the power of attorney and defendants 12 to 17 produced some rent receipts. Both sides also produced oral evidence regarding their respective claim of possession. 

 5. The learned Munsif in consideration of all the oral and documentary evidence of both the parties found that the plaintiffs have title and possession in the suit land and that the defendants have no title or possession in schedules Ga and Gha lands and also that the defendants did not dispute the plaintiffs' claim of title and possession regarding schedules Ka and K ha nor claimed any title therein. He also found that there was cause of action for the claim of injunction and that the suit was maintainable. Upon such findings he decreed the suit. 6. On appeal the learned Additional District Judge noticed the fact that the defendants did not have any claim of right or possession in respect of schedules Ka and 

 Kha. He however found that tee the defendant No. 18 claimed right and possessive in schedules Ga lands on the basis of power of Attorney and since the defendants 12 to 17 claimed right and possession in schedule Gha lands by claiming the same to be their paternal property so there was a complicated question of title and in such a position when the plaintiffs did not bring the suit for declaration of title the simple suit for injunction was not maintain-able. The relevant findings of the learned Additional Judge were as follows :—"The question of title was seriously involved and it was made complicated when the defendant-appellants claimed the same (referring to the schedule Ga land) on the basis of power of Attorney from those owners Shyamapada and Kalipad a  It shows that the question of title is seriously involved in this suit and the plaintiff-respondents cannot succeed in such a test suit 

 7. The learned Additional District Judge having thus found the suit to be unmaintainable did not bother himself to consider either the question of title or the question of possession and dismissed the suit simply on the ground of unmaintainability after setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif. Mr. Azizul Hoq the learned Advocate for the appellants submitted that the learned Additional District Judge committed error of law in finding the suit to be unmaintainable only because questions of title were involved in the suit and declaration of title was not sought. He further submitted that the learned Additional District Judge did not at all consider the oral and documentary evidence regarding the title and possession of the parties and committed error thereby in dismissing the suit without giving any reasons to discard the findings of the learned Munsif. 

 8. On, the other hand Mr. Md. Ansar Ali, the learned Advocate for the respondents supported the findings of the learned Additional District Judge upon the contention that the plaintiffs could not maintain the simple suit for injunction without seeking a declaration of their title which was disputed by the defendants. 

 9. It must be said at once that the learned Additional District Judge was under a total misconception of law when he found that without seeking the declaration of title a simple suit for permanent injunction was not maintainable. Similarly he was also under a misconception of law when he found that because the defendants disputed the title of the plaintiffs and claimed their own title in schedules Ga and Gha lands so a simple suit for injunction was not maintainable. But law nowhere enjoins that a suit for permanent injunction cannot be maintained without seeking a declaration of title only because questions of title are raised. As in a partition suit so also in a suit for injunction questions of title may well be raised but that does not mean that without seeking declaration of title a simple suit for partition or a simple suit for injunction cannot be maintained when the plaintiffs are in possession of the lands. The fact that the question of title also may have to be incidentally gone into in deciding whether the injunction can be given or not is in no way a justification for holding that the suit must be for a declaration of title and for injunction. There can also be no objection as to the maintainability of the suit only for an injunction. Where the allegations of the plaintiffs are that they are in lawful possession of the property and such possession is threatened to be interfered with by the defendants they are well entitled to sue for mere injunction. Where however it is found that the possession of the land is with the defendants or that the plaintiffs had no legal possession in that case of course a suit for mere permanent injunction can be maintained. In the present case the plaintiffs asserted their title and possession in all the lands of schedules Ka to Gha on the basis of kabalas produced by them while on behalf of the defendants there was no claim of title and possession in respect of schedules Ka and Kha but on behalf of defendant No. 18 there was a claim of title and possession in schedule Ga only and the defendants 12 to 17 had their claim in res-pect of schedule Gha only. 

 10. In such case, the duty of the court was to consider all the evidence of both parties and then to ascertain whether the plaintiffs had clear possession in the suit lands and also if such possession was legal and bonafide and after such findings to decide whether a permanent injunction ought to be granted or not. As I have already observed the learned Munsif considered all the documentary evidence of both the parties and found that the plaintiffs had title in all the schedule lands and defendants had no title therein amt also the learned Munsif found that the plaintiffs were in possession of the suit land and the defendants had no possession therein. So it was the duty of the learned Additional District Judge as the final court of fact to reassess the evidence and to find if the plaintiffs had clear possession in the suit land and if such possession was a legal possession being based on title and after such finding he should have considered whether the decree for permanent injunction should be passed or not. But the learned Additional District Judge did not at all consider this issue and did not at all look into the evidence to give any finding on the factual merit of the case but dismissed the suit is a preliminary way en an erroneous view of law that a suit for injunction cannot be maintained only because questions of title are involved. Thus it is found that the learned Additional District Judge erred in law and acted without jurisdiction in dismissing the suit without considering its factual merit. The case has therefore to be remanded to the learned Additional District Judge for deciding the appeal afresh in accordance with law and in the light of the observations made above.
